idiom_name: Result<Success, Failure> plus the competing throws/Error realization
implementation_notes: Swift has two realizations of the same contract: a throwing function (func f() throws -> T with do/catch) for ordinary control flow, and Result<Success, Failure> in the standard library when the outcome must be stored, passed to a callback or composed - map, flatMap, mapError and get() (which converts back to a throwing expression) are the combinators. Failure must conform to Error, so the reason is a typed error value or enum rather than a string, and init(catching:) is the boundary that turns a throwing call into a value. Use Result where the failure cannot be thrown to the caller; use throws where it can.
pitfalls: Result requires Failure: Error, so a non-error reason must be wrapped in an Error enum - usually the right thing, but it makes the reason a type rather than free text.
Mixing channels: a function that returns Result but calls try internally must convert with Result { try ... } or init(catching:), otherwise the error escapes the contract.
try?/as? flatten the error into nil, which is the Swift unwrap: when the reason matters, use try with an explicit catch or mapError.
Equality and hashing apply only when both parameters are Equatable/Hashable, so asserting on results in tests requires equatable error types with equatable associated values.
